title: Receiving well
hookLine: receive gladly, and let the giver see it (On Benefits 2.22)

cards: Someone picks up the check, and you lunge for it. Someone says your talk went well, and you list three things that went wrong.
A neighbor brings soup when you're sick, and the first thing out of your mouth is, oh, you really shouldn't have, and the second is, I'll make it up to you. It sounds polite. It looks modest.
Seneca, still in On Benefits, thinks it can be a quiet way of refusing the gift. Yesterday was the giver's half. Today is the harder half.

teach.b: Be careful about whose favors you accept, Seneca says, even more careful than a giver is about whom to give to, because a benefit ties you to the giver.

Take help from someone you don't respect, and you carry that tie around. Second, let the giver see it. When we accept, we should accept cheerfully and let our gladness show, so the giver gets an immediate return.
Not a muttered thanks at the floor. A face that's actually glad. Third, the first installment.
Whoever receives a benefit gratefully, Seneca says, has already paid the first installment on it. You can't always repay a favor in kind; some you never can.

teach.h: GLAD RECEIVING PAYS THE FIRST PART.
teach.b: But receiving it gladly is a real part of the repayment, open to everyone, right away. Fourth, don't rush to pay it back.
Someone too eager to repay, he warns, acts like an unwilling debtor, as if the favor were a weight to throw off fast.

teach.h: DON'T RACE TO EVEN THE SCORE.
teach.b: Racing to even the score can be a way of saying, I didn't want to owe you.

So the person who lunges for the check isn't always being kind. Sometimes they're refusing to let someone else be kind. Seneca borrows a picture from the older Stoic Chrysippus: two people playing catch.
The giver throws well, the receiver catches well, and the ball has to be caught before it can be thrown back.

how: Some readers of On Benefits practice accepting help and compliments openly, thanking the giver with visible gladness instead of deflecting or rushing to repay.

o: politely refusing so you won't owe anyone
repaying a favor as fast as you possibly can
accepting a gift gladly, letting the giver see it

s: Seneca says rushing to repay a favor is the best way to show gratitude
he says someone too eager to repay acts like an unwilling debtor.
Seneca says receiving a benefit gladly already pays part of it back
the first installment, available to anyone, right away.
Seneca says accept a favor from anyone who offers one
he says to choose carefully whom you're willing to owe.

games.q: a coworker quietly covers your shift so you can get to a family event. what fits On Benefits?
o: insist on paying them back by the end of the week.
thank them warmly, let them see you're glad, and remember it.
play it down, so they don't feel you owe them.
games.why: receive cheerfully and let your gladness show, Seneca says. that's the first installment, and the remembering is the rest.

practice: Bring back a gift you received recently and deflected: a compliment you argued with, help you waved away, a kindness you rushed to repay.
Replay it, and this time just receive it, let your face show you're glad, say thank you, and stop there. Notice whether that feels exposed, and what it might give back to the other person.

wordCard.voice: Receiving well. Seneca says a gift received gladly, with the gladness showing, is already the first installment of the repayment. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: pleasing, and also grateful. Seneca's line uses its adverb: whoever receives grate, gratefully, has paid the first installment.

carryVoice: Your line: receive gladly. Letting someone be kind to you is a kindness too. Until tomorrow.
